title: Shinnecock Hills
summary: Shinnecock Hills is sacred Shinnecock land and a burial landscape with ancestors present for thousands of years. The hills also sit at the center of later land-loss history, preservation fights, and public disputes over development, golf, and recognition of Shinnecock land rights.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Despite holding the remains of Indigenous ancestors buried there for over three thousand years, the sacred Shinnecock Hills were illegally seized by Southampton town officials in 1859 through forged signatures and deceit. Acknowledging this blatant theft underscores the painful realities of colonial dispossession while highlighting the Shinnecock Nation's modern, federally recognized fight to reclaim their ancestral sovereignty and stolen homelands.
history_content:
The Shinnecock Nation built electronic billboard monuments along Sunrise Highway as an assertion of sovereign economic rights on Shinnecock territory. Opposition from Southampton civic groups and state officials led to legal and political conflict, while the Nation defended its authority to build and benefit from the project.

translation_content:
Why Place Names Matter

“Efforts to rename are often resisted because attachment to a name has become part of a sense of belonging to a place. As in names for people, identity and place become intertwined.”

— Robin Kearns, Why Māori Renaming Is the New Norming (2023), Article text

Place-name history should show Native people as active and present, not only as names in old documents.
land_loss_content: In 1998, Shinnecock Tribal Council member Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile publicly connected contemporary land advocacy to the Shinnecock Hills and to Shinnecock lands before the 1859 dispossession.1
